{{Short description|Mass of an astrophysical system}}
In [[Astrophysics|astrophysic]]s, the '''virial mass''' is the mass of a gravitationally bound astrophysical system, assuming the [[virial theorem]] applies. In the context of [[Galaxy formation and evolution|galaxy formation]] and [[dark matter halo]]s, the virial mass is defined as the mass enclosed within the virial radius <math>r_{\rm vir}</math> of a gravitationally bound system, a radius within which the system obeys the virial theorem. The virial radius is determined using a "top-hat" model. A spherical "top hat" density perturbation destined to become a galaxy begins to expand, but the expansion is halted and reversed due to the mass collapsing under gravity until the sphere reaches equilibrium – it is said to be ''virialized''. Within this radius, the sphere obeys the virial theorem which says that the average [[kinetic energy]] is equal to minus one half times the average [[potential energy]], <math>\langle T \rangle = -\frac{1}{2} \langle U \rangle</math>, and this radius defines the virial radius.

== Virial radius ==

The virial radius of a gravitationally bound astrophysical system is the radius within which the virial theorem applies. It is defined as the radius at which the density is equal to the critical density <math>\rho_c</math> of the universe at the redshift of the system, multiplied by an overdensity constant <math>\Delta_c</math>:

<math display="block">\rho(<r_{\rm vir}) = \Delta_c \rho_c(t)=\Delta_{c}\frac{3 H^2(t)}{8 \pi G},</math>

where <math>\rho(<r_{\rm vir})</math> is the halo's mean density within that radius, <math>\Delta_c</math> is a parameter, <math>\rho_{c}(t) = \frac{3 H^2(t)}{8 \pi G}</math> is the [[Critical density (cosmology)|critical density]] of the Universe, <math>H^2(t)=H_0^2[\Omega_r(1+z)^4+\Omega_m(1+z)^3+(1-\Omega_{tot})(1+z)^2+\Omega_{\Lambda}]</math> is the [[Hubble parameter]], and <math>r_{\rm vir}</math> is the virial radius.<ref name=":22">{{Cite book|title=Galaxies and the Universe|url=https://archive.org/details/galaxiesuniverse00spar|url-access=limited|last1=Sparke|first1=Linda S.|author-link=Linda Sparke|last2=Gallagher|first2=John S.|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2007|isbn=978-0-521-67186-6|location=United States of America|pages=[https://archive.org/details/galaxiesuniverse00spar/page/n340 329], 331, 362}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{cite journal|last=White|first=M|date=3 February 2001|title=The mass of a halo|journal=Astronomy and Astrophysics|volume=367|issue=1|pages=27–32|arxiv=astro-ph/0011495|bibcode=2001A&A...367...27W|doi=10.1051/0004-6361:20000357|s2cid=18709176}}</ref> The time dependence of the Hubble parameter indicates that the [[redshift]] of the system is important, as the Hubble parameter changes with time: today's Hubble parameter, referred to as the [[Hubble's law|Hubble constant]] <math>H_0</math>, is not the same as the Hubble parameter at an earlier time in the Universe's history, or in other words, at a different redshift. The overdensity <math>\Delta_c</math> is approximated by
<math display="block">\Delta_c \approx 18\pi^2+82x-39x^2,</math>
where <math display="inline">x=\Omega_m(z)-1</math>, <math>\Omega_m(z)=\frac{\Omega_0(1+z)^3}{E(z)^2},</math> <math>\Omega_0=\Omega_m(0)=\frac{8 \pi G \rho_0}{3 H_0^2},</math> and <math>E(z)=\frac{H(z)}{H_0}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Bryan|first1=Greg L.|last2=Norman|first2=Michael L.|year=1998|title=Statistical Properties of X-ray Clusters: Analytic and Numerical Comparisons|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=495|issue=80|pages=80|arxiv=astro-ph/9710107|doi=10.1086/305262|bibcode=1998ApJ...495...80B|s2cid=16118077}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|title=Galaxy Formation and Evolution|url=https://archive.org/details/galaxyformatione00moho_818|url-access=limited|last1=Mo|first1=Houjun|last2=van den Bosch|first2=Frank|last3=White|first3=Simon|publisher=Cambridge University Press|year=2011|isbn=978-0-521-85793-2|location=United States of America|pages=[https://archive.org/details/galaxyformatione00moho_818/page/n257 236]}}</ref> Since it depends on the [[density parameter]] of matter <math>\Omega_m(z)</math>, its value depends on the cosmological model used. In an [[Einstein–de Sitter universe|Einstein–de Sitter model]] it equals <math>18\pi^2\approx 178</math>. This definition is not universal, however, as the exact value of <math>\Delta_c</math> depends on the cosmology. In an Einstein–de Sitter model, it is assumed that the density parameter is due to matter only, where <math>\Omega_m=1</math>. Compare this to the currently accepted cosmological model for the universe, [[ΛCDM]] model, where <math>\Omega_m=0.3</math> and <math>\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7</math>; in this case, <math>\Delta_c \approx 100</math> (at a redshift of zero; with increased redshift the value approaches the Einstein-de Sitter value and then drops to a value of 56.65 for an empty [[de Sitter universe]]). Nevertheless, it is typically assumed that <math>\Delta_c = 200</math> for the purpose of using a common definition, also giving the correct one-digit rounding for a long period 1090 > ''z'' > 0.87, and this is denoted as <math>r_{200}</math> for the virial radius and <math>M_{200}</math> for the virial mass. Using this convention, the mean density is given by
<math display="block">\rho(<r_{200}) = 200  \rho_c(t)=200\frac{3 H^2(t)}{8 \pi G}.</math>

Other conventions for the overdensity constant include <math>\Delta_c = 500</math>, or <math>\Delta_c = 1000</math>, depending on the type of analysis being done, in which case the virial radius and virial mass is signified by the relevant subscript.<ref name=":12" />

== Defining the virial mass ==

Given the virial radius and the overdensity convention, the virial mass <math>M_{\rm vir}</math> can be found through the relation

<math display="block">M_{\rm vir}=\frac{4}{3}\pi r_{\rm vir}^3 \rho(<r_{\rm vir})=\frac{4}{3}\pi r_{\rm vir}^3 \Delta_c \rho_{c}.</math>If the convention that <math>\Delta_c = 200</math> is used, then this becomes<ref name=":22" /><math display="block">M_{200}=\frac{4}{3}\pi r_{200}^3 200 \rho_{c}=\frac{100 r_{200}^3 H^2(t)}{G},</math>where <math>H(t)</math> is the Hubble parameter as described above, and G is the [[gravitational constant]]. This defines the virial mass of an astrophysical system.

== Applications to dark matter halos ==
Given <math>    M_{200}</math> and <math>r_{200}</math>, properties of dark matter halos can be defined, including circular velocity, the density profile, and total mass. <math>    M_{200}</math> and <math>r_{200}</math> are directly related to the [[Navarro–Frenk–White profile|Navarro–Frenk–White]] (NFW) profile, a density profile that describes dark matter halos modeled with the [[cold dark matter]] paradigm. The NFW profile is given by<math display="block">\rho(r)=\frac{\delta_c\rho_{c}}{r/r_s(1+r/r_s)^2},</math>where <math>\rho_c</math> is the critical density, and the overdensity <math>\delta_c=\frac{200}{3}\frac{c_{200}^3}{\ln(1+c_{200})-\frac{c_{200}}{1+c_{200}}}</math> (not to be confused with <math>\Delta_c</math>) and the scale radius <math>r_s</math> are unique to each halo, and the [[concentration parameter]] is given by <math>c_{200}=\frac{r_{200}}{r_s}</math>.<ref name=":02">{{Cite journal|last1=Navarro|first1=Julio F.|last2=Frenk|first2=Carlos S.|last3=White|first3=Simon D. M.|year=1996|title=The Structure of Cold Dark Matter Halos|journal=The Astrophysical Journal|volume=462|pages=563–575|arxiv=astro-ph/9508025|doi=10.1086/177173|bibcode=1996ApJ...462..563N|s2cid=119007675}}</ref> In place of <math>\delta_c\rho_{c}</math>, <math>\rho_s</math> is often used, where <math>\rho_s</math> is a parameter unique to each halo. The total mass of the dark matter halo can then be computed by integrating over the volume of the density out to the virial radius <math>r_{200}</math>:

<math>M=\int \limits_{0}^{r_{200}}4\pi r^2\rho(r)dr=4\pi \rho_s r_s^3[\ln(\frac{r_{200}+r_s}{r_s})-\frac{r_{200}}{r_{200}+r_s}]=4\pi \rho_s r_s^3[\ln(1+c_{200})-\frac{c_{200}}{1+c_{200}}].</math>

From the definition of the circular velocity, <math>V_c(r)=\sqrt{\frac{GM(r)}{r}},</math> we can find the circular velocity at the virial radius <math>r_{200}</math>:<math display="block">V_{200}=\sqrt{\frac{GM_{200}}{r_{200}}}.</math>Then the circular velocity for the dark matter halo is given by<math display="block">V_c^2(r)=V_{200}^2\frac{1}{x}\frac{\ln(1+cx)-(cx)/(1+cx)}{\ln(1+c)-c/(1+c)},</math>where <math>x=r/r_{200}</math>.<ref name=":02" />

Although the NFW profile is commonly used, other profiles like the [[Einasto profile]] and profiles that take into account the adiabatic contraction of the dark matter due to the baryonic content are also used to characterize dark matter halos.

To compute the total mass of the system, including stars, gas, and dark matter, the [[Jeans equations]] need to be used with density profiles for each component.
